beats.intro: Chapter six, lesson seven. Microfilaments and intermediate filaments. [[arm]]Lift your arm, and muscle cells all along it shorten at once. [[amoeba]]A pond amoeba crawls across a slide with no legs at all. [[map]]Both are the work of the cytoskeleton, the scaffolding and rails of the cell, lit up here on our map. [[ask]]Today we meet two of its three kinds of fibre. What are they made of, and how do they make a cell move?
beats.actin: Start with the thinnest fibre. [[rod]]Microfilaments are solid rods, about seven nanometers across. [[helix]]Each one is built from actin subunits, two strands of beads twisted around each other into a helix. [[pull]]Their main structural job is to bear tension, to resist pulling forces, a bit like the cables that hold up a tent. [[cortex]]Just inside the plasma membrane, they form a three-dimensional network called the cortex, which helps support the cell's shape. [[villi]]And in intestinal cells, bundles of microfilaments form the core of microvilli, the tiny fingers that line the gut and soak up food.
beats.muscle: Microfilaments can also drive movement, but never alone. [[myo]]Their partner is myosin, a motor protein. [[parallel]]In a muscle cell, thousands of thin actin filaments run parallel to one another. [[thick]]Thick myosin filaments sit between them, interdigitated, like the fingers of two hands laced together. [[heads]]Myosin heads grip the actin and pull. [[slide]]The filaments slide past each other, the overlap grows, and the whole cell shortens. [[keep]]Notice that neither kind of filament gets shorter. They slide. [[energy]]The heads need energy from the cell to do this work. [[lift]]Repeat that in thousands of cells, and your arm lifts.
beats.q1: Quick check. What happens when a muscle cell contracts?
beats.amoeba: Cells that are not muscle use the same partners. [[amoeba]]An amoeba moves by crawling, called amoeboid movement. [[cortex]]Its outer cytoplasm, the cortex, is a gel held by an actin network. [[inner]]The inner cytoplasm is more fluid. [[contract]]Localized contraction by actin and myosin drives the movement. [[extend]]The cell pushes out a lobe called a pseudopodium, which means false foot. [[crawl]]Then the cell moves toward its pseudopodium, crawling along a surface.
beats.stream: A third job is cytoplasmic streaming. [[leaf]]Inside a leaf cell, the cytoplasm flows around in a circle. [[chloro]]Chloroplasts are carried along like boats on a river. [[drive]]In plant cells, actin and myosin drive the flow, together with changes between a more fluid and a more gel-like cytoplasm. The slides call these sol-gel transformations. [[speed]]The flow speeds up the distribution of materials inside the cell, so nothing has to wait for slow drifting.
beats.scale: One more detail from the figure. Always read the scale bar. [[muscle]]The muscle picture is zoomed right in: its bar is only half a micrometer. [[plant]]The plant cells are bigger, with a bar of thirty micrometers. [[ameba]]And the amoeba picture is zoomed far out: its bar is one hundred micrometers. [[same]]Yet the same two proteins, actin and myosin, work in all three.
beats.inter: Now the third class, intermediate filaments. [[rope]]They are like ropes of protein, eight to twelve nanometers across. [[size]]That is thicker than microfilaments but thinner than microtubules, which is why they are called intermediate. [[job]]They support the shape of the cell, and they fix organelles in place. [[perm]]Of the three kinds, they are the most permanent. The others are taken apart and rebuilt quickly. Intermediate filaments are more stable, though not unchangeable.
beats.compare: Put all three side by side. [[mt]]Microtubules are hollow tubes, the widest of the three, about twenty five nanometers. [[if]]Intermediate filaments come next, eight to twelve. [[mf]]Microfilaments are the thinnest, at seven. [[jobs]]Microtubules are rails for motors. Intermediate filaments are anchors that hold things in place. And microfilaments are cables that pull, push, and shape the cell edge.
beats.q2: Quick check. Put the three fibres in order of width.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Microfilaments are twisted chains of actin, seven nanometers wide. They resist tension and form the cortex. [[w2]]With myosin, they drive muscle contraction, amoeboid movement, and cytoplasmic streaming. [[w3]]Intermediate filaments, eight to twelve nanometers, support cell shape and fix organelles in place, and are the most permanent. [[end]]Now try the practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That's the end of chapter six, lesson seven.
